c.v: This stage turns the runner's smoke test into a scenario about the robot doing something. The route is two goals, in front and then to the side, driven by a follower that turns on the spot before it drives whenever the heading error is large, so a small walled world doesn't turn a wide arc into a wall. Four checks judge the run: every goal reached in order, the robot inside the last goal's tolerance at the end, the time from its first movement to the last goal, and its top speed.
The decision worth defending is that the judge never asks the follower how it did. Every check comes from the samples the runner collected on

, so a follower reporting success while the robot sits still fails anyway, and reaching a goal alone is not enough: a robot that clips the goal circle at speed and drives into a wall has technically arrived, which is why the end position is checked too.

and exits 0 five times running, with tolerances set above the largest of those five measured runs rather than guessed. And it fails in the ways we asked it to: cutting the relay leaves the robot unmoved with the speed check still met, and a tightened time tolerance on the same run gives exactly one failed line.

subs.title: Motion task and its tolerance checks

The smoke scenario drove forward for three seconds. That proved the runner and nothing about the robot: a robot with one wheel locked passes it. Normal operation has to mean that the robot got somewhere, so the task is a list of goals, each with a position tolerance, and the verdict comes from where the robot actually stood.

Two goals, in front and then to the side, so that one run covers driving straight, turning and driving again. In the odometry frame the robot starts at the origin facing along x, so (0.80, 0.00) and then (0.80, 0.50) with a tolerance of 0.10 m keep it inside about one metre of where it spawned. The sandbox world is small; open it in RViz from the frames topic, look at where the walls are, and move the goals closer in if a wall is nearer than a metre. Whatever you choose, write the numbers down: they are the scenario's definition from now on.
The rules of the follower are four sentences:

items.v: a goal counts as reached the first time the robot stands inside its tolerance, and then the next goal starts;
while the goal lies more than
off the robot's heading, turn on the spot and don't drive;

c.v: Turning on the spot first is the part worth arguing about. A differential-drive robot that drives and turns at once follows an arc, and with a large heading error that arc is long and swings wide, which in a small walled world means a wall. Turning first costs a second and keeps the path close to the straight line between the goals, so the position tolerance is about the robot's accuracy rather than about the shape of its approach.

The heading error has to wrap. The difference of two angles can come out as 6.14 rad when the honest answer is 0.14 rad the other way, and a follower that believes the first one turns almost all the way round.
returns the value between -π and π, which is the wrapped angle, and it does it without a loop.

c.v: Read the run rather than the code. The robot drives straight to (0.70, 0.00), which is the first goal's edge and not its centre:

is a tolerance, so the route moves on as soon as the robot is inside the circle. At 4.00 s it is turning on the spot at the full 0.60 rad/s with no forward speed, because the second goal is then about 1.07 rad off its heading, more than five times

and it drives with a small correcting turn. The whole route takes 7.65 s on a robot with no acceleration limit, which is the floor: the real one accelerates, and Build 3 measures what it costs.

That toy robot is worth its ten lines. It is not the simulator and it proves nothing about Gazebo, but it does answer the one question the unit tests can't: put the rules in a loop and does the robot converge, or does it circle the goal forever? Circling is the usual way a follower like this fails, and it shows up here in a millisecond rather than in a 30 second scenario run.

The architecture topic put a controller between the mission and the supervisor: it reads odometry as feedback and publishes
. This is that node. It reads
, and the difference matters in two topics' time: when the relay cuts
, the follower loses its feedback exactly as the supervisor does, which is what a real controller would experience. The runner keeps reading

The follower waits before it drives. It starts counting at its first odometry message and holds still for

of simulated time, 2 s by default. The reason is the runner: its own warm-up is shorter, 1 s, so by the time the robot first moves the runner is already collecting samples. If the robot moved first, the run would be judged from the middle of an acceleration and the time it took would come out short.

items.v: copied in, so that it builds on its own:

c.v: The node has no timer. A command goes out for every odometry message, so the follower runs at the rate of its feedback, about 30 Hz from the TurtleBot's DiffDrive system, and it stops sending the moment the feedback stops. That is the behaviour the missing-odometry scenario wants: a controller starved of feedback should go quiet, and then the supervisor's command timeout is what stops the robot. The stamp on the command is the stamp of the odometry it answers, which makes a recorded run say which measurement produced which command. When every goal is reached the node logs once and sends nothing more, and the supervisor takes over with its stops half a second later.

The judge never asks the follower how it did. Every check is computed from the samples the runner collected on

items.v: every goal was reached, in order;
at the end of the run the robot stood within the last goal's tolerance, so it stopped there rather than driving through;

no sample exceeded the speed limit.

c.v: The third one is measured from the robot's first movement and not from the start of a phase, which keeps the scenario independent of when the follower happens to begin. The second exists because the first alone is weak: a robot that clips the goal circle at speed and carries on into a wall has reached the goal.

It searches for each goal only in the samples at or after the one before it, so the goals have to be reached in order; a robot that wandered through goal 2 on its way to goal 1 gets no credit. When a goal is never reached it stops there, which is why the stalled run reports one goal and leaves the time unmeasured rather than reporting a wrong number. c.v: The runner and the follower read the same three parameters,

That is on purpose: the goals are the scenario's definition, so the node that drives them and the node that judges them must not be able to disagree. c.v: Write down the largest time and the largest distance. The time tolerance goes above the largest you saw with room to spare, and 20 s is a starting point rather than an answer: the toy robot in Build 1 took 7.65 s, and the real one accelerates, brakes at every goal and turns at whatever rate the DiffDrive system gives it. If your largest run is 14 s, a tolerance of 20 s says the scenario fails when something is wrong rather than when the machine is busy. If it is 19 s, raise the tolerance and write down why. The same for the position: the tolerance in the goal decides when the follower stops, so the distance at the end is usually a little under it, and a run that lands within a millimetre of the tolerance means the follower is barely arriving.
